questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Compound Predicate in Symbolic Form
questions.problem:
$x$ is a multiple of $3$ **and** $5.$

Express the compound predicate above in symbolic form given the following notations:

- $P(x):$ $x$ is a multiple of $3$

- $Q(x):$ $x$ is a multiple of $5$
questions.worked_solution:
The word "and" is represented by the symbol "$∧.$"

So, the sentence reads

$$
{{x\text{ is a multiple of }3}_{⏟}}_{P}\,{{\text{and}}_{⏟}}_{∧}\,{{x\text{ is a multiple of }5}_{⏟}}_{Q},
$$

that is, $P∧Q.$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Nested Compound Predicate in Symbolic Form
questions.problem:
$x$ is positive, **and** $x$ is irrational **or** integer.

Express the compound predicate above in symbolic form given the following notations:

- $P(x):$ $x$ is positive

- $Q(x):$ $x$ is irrational

- $R(x):$ $x$ is integer
questions.worked_solution:
The word "and" is represented by the symbol "$∧,$" while the word "or" is represented by the symbol "$∨.$"

Note that this sentence consists of two parts:

- **Part 1:** $x$ is positive. This corresponds to $P.$

- **Part 2:** $x$ is irrational or integer. This corresponds to

$$
{{x\text{ is irrational}}_{⏟}}_{Q}\,{{\text{or}}_{⏟}}_{∨}\,{{x\text{ is integer}}_{⏟}}_{R},
$$

that is, $Q∨R.$

So, we can express the sentence as

$$
{{x\text{ is positive}}_{⏟}}_{P}\,{{\text{and}}_{⏟}}_{∧}\,{{x\text{ is irrational}\text{ or integer}}_{⏟}}_{Q\,∨\,R},
$$

that is, $P∧(Q∨R).$

questions.problem:
$n$ is negative **or** greater than $10,$ **and** $n$ is odd.

Express the compound predicate above in symbolic form given the following notations:

- $N(n):$ $n$ is negative

- $G(n):$ $n$ is greater than $10,$

- $O(n):$ $n$ is odd
questions.worked_solution:
The word "and" is represented by the symbol "$∧,$" while the word "or" is represented by the symbol "$∨.$"

Note that this sentence consists of two parts: 

- **Part 1:** $n$  is negative or greater than $10.$  This corresponds to

$$
{{n\text{ is negative }}_{⏟}}_{N}\,{{\text{or}}_{⏟}}_{∨}\,{{n\text{ is greater than }10}_{⏟}}_{G},
$$

that is, $N∨G.$

- **Part 2:** $n$ is odd. This corresponds to $O.$

So, we can express the sentence as

$$
{{n\text{ is negative }\text{ or }\text{ greater than }10}_{⏟}}_{N∨G}\,{{\text{and}}_{⏟}}_{∧}\,{{n\text{ is odd }}_{⏟}}_{O},
$$

that is, $(N∨G)∧O.$

The shaded regions above represent the truth sets of the predicates $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y),$ defined over the universal set ${R}^{2}.$ Which of the following is the truth set of $P∨Q?$
questions.worked_solution:
The truth set of $P∨Q$ represents the *union* of the truth sets of $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y):$

$$

$$

Therefore, to get the truth set of $P(x,y)∨Q(x,y),$ we take all the points that belong to ${T}_{P}$ or ${T}_{Q},$ as shown below.

**Note:** The points where the *dashed* line meets the *solid* curve belong to ${T}_{P}\cup {T}_{Q}$ since these points lie in ${T}_{Q}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Truth Sets of Conjunctions and Disjunctions
questions.problem:
Find the truth set of $P(x)∧Q(x)$ given the following predicates defined over the set of positive integers:

- $P(x):$ $x$ is even

- $Q(x):$ $x$ is less than $9$
questions.worked_solution:
The truth set of $P(x)∧Q(x)$ represents the *intersection* of the truth sets of $P(x)$ and $Q(x):$

$$
{T}_{P∧Q}={T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q}
$$

We start by finding the truth sets of $P(x)$ and $Q(x):$

- The truth set of $P(x)$ is the set of all even positive integers, i.e.,

$$
{T}_{P}={2,4,6,8,10,…}.
$$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is 

$$
{T}_{Q}={1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P∧Q} & ={T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q} \\  & ={2,4,6,8,10,…}\cap {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8} \\  & ={2,4,6,8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Simplify the following sentence: $x$ is even and it is an even number, or $x$ is even or it divides $11.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we simplify the phrase "$x$ is even and it is an even number" to just "$x$ is even." The sentence now reads

"$x$ is even, or $x$ is even or it divides $11.$"

Then, using the associative law, we can move the comma in the sentence:

"$x$ is even or $x$ is even, or it divides $11.$"

Now, we simplify the phrase "$x$ is even or $x$ is even" to just "$x$ is even." The sentence now reads

"$x$ is even, or it divides $11.$"

Finally, we simplify the sentence to

"$x$ is even or it divides $11.$"

choices.value: $x$ is even or it divides $11$ but not both

canonical_examples.worked_solution:

So, the second sentence reads

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing a Nested Compound Predicate in Symbolic Form
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following compound predicate:

$x$ is positive **and** a multiple of $4,$ **or** $x$ is negative.

Express this compound predicate in symbolic form given the following notations:

- $P(x):$ $x$ is positive

- $M(x):$ $x$ is a multiple of $4$

- $N(x):$ $x$ is negative
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The word "and" is represented by the symbol "$\land,$" while the word "or" is represented by the symbol "$\lor.$"

Note that this sentence consists of two parts:

- **Part 1:** $x$ is positive and a multiple of $4.$ This corresponds to

$$
\underbrace{x \,\textrm{is positive}}_P \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textrm{and}}_{\land} \quad \underbrace{x \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is a multiple of }4 }_M,
$$

that is, $P \land M.$

- **Part 2:** $x$ is negative. This corresponds to $N.$

So, we can express the sentence as

$$
\underbrace{x \,\textrm{ is positive}\,\textrm{and a multiple of }4 }_{P \land M} \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textrm{or}}_{\lor} \quad \underbrace{x \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is negative} }_N,
$$

that is, $(P \land M) \lor N.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Truth Sets of Conjunctions and Disjunctions
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the truth set of $P(x) \lor Q(x)$ given the following predicates defined over the universal set $\mathbb{R}{:}$

- $P(x):$ $3x -1 < 5$

- $Q(x):$ $x \geq 3$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The truth set of $P(x) \lor Q(x)$ represents the *union* of the truth sets of $P(x)$ and $Q(x){:}$

$$
T_{P \lor Q} = T_P \cup T_Q
$$

We start by finding the truth sets of $P(x)$ and $Q(x){:}$

- To find the the truth set of $P(x),$ we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-1 & <5 \\ 3x & <6 \\ x & <2\end{aligned}
$$

 
So, the truth set of $P(x)$ is
$T_P = (-\infty,2).$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is 
$T_Q = [3,\infty).$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P∨Q} & ={T}_{P}\cup {T}_{Q} \\  & =(-\infty ,2)\cup [3,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$
